title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit of conservative contamination detectors (exact token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) on a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample to test whether deterministic guarded exclusions change validator‑measured success rates. The run used a single hosted LLM (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") and a deterministic NetOps validator. Execution sampled provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated deterministically and applied shared_initial_candidate semantics so baseline and guarded episodes reused a single generation when no high‑confidence flags occurred. No preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags were produced; all 150 baseline and 150 guarded episodes passed the validator (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We reconcile the preregistration→execution trace: the synthetic provenance and shared‑generation semantics materially limited the audit's sensitivity to generation‑level contamination in this run. We present artifact‑grounded lessons and concrete design changes (provenance‑rich sampling, independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model scope, per‑item detector reporting, paraphrase‑robust detectors, and matched power calculations) to increase audit sensitivity for web‑sourced benchmarks.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent‑to‑configuration translation and automated configuration repair. Operational adoption hinges on reliable, evidence‑bounded evaluation: inflated benchmark scores caused by dataset contamination (items or templates that leak into model training data) or by low‑complexity templated tasks can mislead deployers and researchers. Recent surveys and benchmarks have highlighted both the promise of LLMs for NetOps and persistent evaluation‑validity risks, motivating contamination‑aware audit protocols that pair deterministic verifiers with precommitted contamination detectors.

Research question and contribution. We preregistered and executed an artifact‑anchored confirmatory audit to answer: under a conservative detector suite (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered thresholds; provenance timestamp heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence contamination flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying those controls change an LLM's validator pass rate? Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered confirmatory experiment (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) executed end‑to‑end and archived; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces; and (3) an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation grounded in archived execution artifacts explaining why the run produced a degenerate null and prescribing concrete audit design changes to increase sensitivity in future studies.

Scope, key execution facts, and bounded claims. Two execution facts materially bound inference from this run. First, the confirmatory sample used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated deterministically (task_manifest entries carry source_identifier values with the "synthetic-netops:" prefix). Second, execution semantics employed shared_initial_candidate generation (independent_condition_generation = false): when no high‑confidence exclusions occur, a single shared model generation per item serves both baseline and guarded episodes. Both facts are recorded in the archived execution artifacts (for example, execution/model_configuration.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl). These archived facts mechanically limit the audit's sensitivity to detect generation‑level contamination under the executed regime; we therefore restrict claims to the executed synthetic sampling and shared‑generation semantics and do not extrapolate to web‑sourced benchmarks or to other generation regimes.
sections.related_work:
LLM-assisted NetOps and verification. Recent work demonstrates that LLMs can produce useful configuration artifacts in constrained settings and that integrating deterministic verifiers or iterative validate–repair loops improves average repair quality [https://openalex.org/W7162218766, https://openalex.org/W7157506260]. Deterministic verification frameworks (e.g., Header Space Analysis and localized subspecification approaches) are practical oracles for reachability and policy checks and are commonly integrated into generate–validate pipelines [http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.300.8659, https://openalex.org/W2742515467].

Evaluation validity and contamination risk. Meta‑studies and surveys catalog key evaluation threats for LLMs—hallucination, templating, and dataset contamination—and recommend contamination‑aware benchmark design, deterministic provenance checks, and auditor transparency [https://openalex.org/W4404534210, https://openalex.org/W7166900660]. Benchmarks that focus on templated tasks or reused prompts can overstate model capability; conversely, validator‑backed functional checks can provide operationally meaningful pass/fail outcomes but only if audit sampling and detector sensitivity are aligned with the suspected contamination modes [https://openalex.org/W4404602270].

Positioning. Unlike broad capability benchmarks that report absolute model scores, our study is a preregistered audit of contamination defenses applied to a reproducible sample with an oracle validator. The contribution is methodological: an artifact‑anchored protocol, a preregistration→execution reconciliation, and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations to improve audit sensitivity for real‑world, web‑sourced benchmarks.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered as study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) computed across item×model pairs; confirmatory inference uses an exact two‑sided McNemar test and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) executed by the archived paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor.

Detectors and guarded policy (preregistered). The preregistered detector suite comprised: (1) exact normalized token equality after canonicalization; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap (Jaccard/overlap) with prespecified high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 and sensitivity checks at 0.65 and 0.50; and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item source timestamps to the model public cutoff. The guarded policy deterministically excludes high‑confidence flagged items (exact match OR fuzzy overlap ≥ 0.80) and replaces them via deterministic retemplating/topology‑augmentation from the same generator distribution, subject to preregistered embedding‑similarity acceptance rules. These transformation semantics and replacement rules are recorded in the archived transformation_manifest.json and preregistration artifacts.

Sampling, generation semantics, and critical execution choices. The preregistration permitted deterministic task generators for reproducibility but required explicit recording of generation semantics. The executed run used deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 to produce synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate): if no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, the same model output was reused for baseline and guarded episodes. This choice reduced model calls (model_calls_used = 150) and meant that variance between conditions could only arise if the contamination detectors triggered replacements. The planning contract (maximum_model_calls = 300) and actual model call accounting are archived in execution/model_configuration.json and the execution manifest.

Validator and scoring rule. The verification oracle is deterministic_netops_validator_v5; for each episode it performs parse→state update→property checks and produces a binary pass/fail plus a detailed validator_trace (fields such as parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, and explicit violation codes). The prespecified scoring rule for intent→configuration tasks was full_intent_constraint_validation: the generated configuration must yield the intended final state while respecting workflow policy constraints. Representative validator traces are archived under execution/scoring.

Analysis plan and prespecified sensitivities. The primary confirmatory analysis followed the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor. Prespecified sensitivity analyses included: (a) treating failed model calls as failures; (b) repeating fuzzy‑overlap checks at thresholds 0.50 and 0.65; and (c) subgrouping by templated vs realistic items via a templating detector. The preregistration included power guidance noting that a single‑model, single‑call design reduces detectable effect size versus a multi‑model plan; those power constraints are discussed in Recommendations.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. The execution completed the planned episode count of 300 episodes (150 item pairs) with zero failed episodes. Because shared_initial_candidate was in effect and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, the run used one shared model generation per item (model_calls_used = 150 rather than the preregistered maximum of 300). Deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm complete_pair_count = 150 and consistent provider call accounting (provider call audit recorded completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 150). These accounting facts are archived in the execution manifest and reconciliation artifacts.

Contamination detectors and flagged episodes. Under the preregistered conservative detectors, the execution produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags: analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged episode rows. This empty flag set is an archived artifact of the run; it reflects the interaction between the detector thresholds and the sampled items' provenance and surface form. Importantly, the archived detector workflow recorded detailed fuzzy overlap outputs only for episodes that met flagging criteria or required replacement handling; because no episodes reached the high‑confidence threshold there is no archived distribution of per‑item overlap scores to report. We therefore report the artifact‑documented absence of high‑confidence flags rather than inventing per‑item overlap statistics.

Validator outcomes and primary confirmatory statistics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for every baseline episode (baseline_success_count = 150/150, baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for every guarded episode (guarded_success_count = 150/150, guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All per‑episode validator traces and scoring records are archived in the execution bundle.

Representative exemplar and validator trace. A representative archived episode (pair‑000001 / task‑000001) illustrates the artifact structure and validator trace: the normalized reference and normalized_response are identical (four required commands) and the validator returned score = 1 with parsed_command_count = 4 and violation_count = 0. This exemplar (execution/responses/task-000001-*.txt and execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json) demonstrates the format and content of the archived traces used to compute the confirmatory statistics.

Absence of overlap score aggregates and interpretation. Because the preregistered detector recorded overlap details only when a flag or replacement occurred, the archive does not contain a per‑item summary distribution of fuzzy 5‑gram overlap scores for this run. This archived absence implies we cannot report descriptive statistics (min/median/percentiles) for overlap distances in this sample; the artifact‑grounded fact is that no overlaps met the high‑confidence threshold and therefore no replacement workflows recorded overlap metadata.
sections.discussion:
Why the run produced a degenerate paired outcome. Two artifact‑verified execution facts explain the degenerate null: (1) the sample consisted of provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated deterministically (task_manifest entries with source_identifier starting "synthetic-netops:"), so canonicalized exact matches and high 5‑gram overlaps with public corpus fingerprints were unlikely; and (2) independent_condition_generation was false (shared_initial_candidate semantics), so when no high‑confidence flags occurred the same generation served both baseline and guarded episodes. Both facts are archived in execution/model_configuration.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl and together produced identical paired outputs per item, making the paired test uninformative for generation‑level contamination detection in this run.

What the execution answers and what remains unresolved. The execution answers a narrowly circumscribed methodological question under the executed regime: given provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and the preregistered conservative detectors, do high‑confidence flags occur and do guarded exclusions change validator pass rates? For this sampling and execution semantics the answer is no. The execution does not estimate contamination prevalence in independent public web‑sourced benchmarks, cannot detect paraphrase‑style leakage escaping n‑gram detectors, and cannot measure cross‑model contamination signals; those remain open empirical questions requiring different sampling and generation semantics.

Practical audit design lessons (artifact‑grounded). The preregistration and execution artifacts together motivate the following concrete design changes to increase audit sensitivity for web‑sourced benchmarks: (a) sample provenance‑rich public items (rather than synthetic items) so detectors can exercise real training‑corpus overlap modes; (b) set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded outputs are independently generated and cannot collapse to a shared output; (c) expand to multiple models and independent seeds to increase observable discordance and enable cross‑model contamination signals; (d) record per‑item fuzzy overlap scores regardless of flag status to permit overlap distribution reporting; and (e) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and manual adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows from artifacts: the execution manifest, reconciliation checks, and the empty contamination_summary that together show how the current choices limited detector exercise.

Operational implications for NetOps benchmarking. For practitioners, the audit illustrates that verifier‑backed validators remain valuable functional oracles, but audit sensitivity depends critically on sampling provenance and generation semantics. Contamination audits intended to assess public benchmark leakage should avoid purely synthetic provenance and shared‑generation modes and should commit to reporting per‑item detector outputs to enable forensic follow‑up and threshold sensitivity analysis.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed an artifact‑anchored, confirmatory contamination audit on a 150‑pair NetOps sample using conservative deterministic detectors and a deterministic validator. The execution produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded), yielding a paired difference of 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar p = 1.0). The degenerate null result is artifact‑supported and stems from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics; it does not imply absence of contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks. We provide an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation, artifact‑grounded recommendations to improve audit sensitivity (provenance‑rich sampling, independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model scope, per‑item detector reporting, paraphrase‑robust detectors, and matched power calculations), and a full archived execution bundle documenting the run. Future audits that adopt these changes will be better positioned to detect contamination effects in operational, web‑sourced NetOps benchmarks.

After the autonomy lock, the AI system autonomously performed literature search, gap selection, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, peer‑review simulation, and revision. The execution archive includes model configuration and task manifest artifacts (e.g., execution/model_configuration.json and execution/task_manifest.jsonl) that record critical execution semantics (including independent_condition_generation = false and the use of provenance‑stable synthetic tasks). No manual human editing of technical content, analyses, references, figures, tables, captions, or this Disclosure Statement occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development and rehearsal runs occurred but their artifacts were not used as empirical evidence for this final study unless independently re‑created under the locked pipeline.
limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require paraphrase‑robust detectors and manual adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
